title: Why the old king bows
hookLine: King Pasenadi kisses the Buddha's feet and tells why he loves the community

lines: THE FIVE SIGNS OF A KING, HANDED OVER.
cards: King Pasenadi again, but much older now. He's out driving through a park, and the trees are quiet and beautiful, the kind of quiet that makes him think of the Buddha.
He asks where the Buddha is staying: a fair way off, in a Sakyan town. He goes anyway.
At the monastery, he takes off the five signs of a king, the sword, the sunshade, the crown and the rest, and hands them to his general. Then he walks alone to a closed door, coughs, and knocks.

teach.h: I AM PASENADI, KING OF KOSALA.
teach.b: The Buddha opens the door. And the king of Kosala goes down on the floor, puts his head at the Buddha's feet, kisses them, strokes them, and says his own name: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala.
The Buddha asks, why such honor? The king tells him, reason after reason.
I see your monks living together in harmony, like milk and water, looking at one another with kind eyes. I don't always see that, he says, even among brothers and sisters.
I sit in judgment in my own court, and people interrupt me.
When you teach hundreds of people, there isn't a sound. Once someone coughed, and the person beside him nudged him: quiet, the Teacher is speaking.

Clever people come to trap you with questions, and leave as your followers. My own two chamberlains, men I feed and pay, lie with their heads toward you at night, and their feet toward me. Then the most personal one.
The Buddha is a noble, and so am I. He's of Kosala, and so am I.

teach.h: HE'S EIGHTY, AND SO AM I.
teach.b: He's eighty, and so am I. That's why I bow. After the king leaves, the Buddha calls these the king's monuments to the Dhamma, and tells the monks to learn them.
A king listing, not miracles or doctrines, but behavior: how monks look at each other, how a room stays quiet, where servants point their heads. The commentaries add a sadder frame.
While the king was inside, his general rode off with the royal insignia, and Pasenadi never sat on his throne again. Which makes his last reason, both of us are eighty, all the more tender.

how: Buddhists bow to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, often three times, at shrines, temples and before teachers, and many describe the bow as an expression of gratitude for what they have seen the practice do.

o: a royal shrine that holds the Buddha's relics
a monument to the Dhamma, like the king's reasons
the five signs of a king, laid aside

games.q: the king's reasons: tap the pairs.
p: not a sound, not even a cough
sleep with their heads toward the Buddha

s: Pasenadi kept his crown and sword on when he went in
he handed the five royal insignia to his general first.
the king's reasons are mostly about miracles
they're about behavior: harmony, quiet, and how people act.
the Buddha called the king's reasons monuments to the Dhamma
and told the monks to learn them.

games.q: you're an old king at the Buddha's door. he asks why you honor him so deeply. what does Pasenadi talk about?
o: what he's seen: harmony, silence, and two old men the same age
games.why: everything Pasenadi lists is something he observed: monks like milk and water, a silent room, and 'he's eighty, and so am I.'

practice: Ask yourself, like the king, what you've actually seen in your own life that makes this path worth walking: not a doctrine, but something noticed, a calmer morning, a kinder reply, a person whose way of living moved you.
Name two or three quietly, the way Pasenadi counted his, and rest with them.

wordCard.voice: Dhammacetiya. Pasenadi, at eighty, kisses the Buddha's feet and gives his reasons: harmony, quiet, and things he'd seen with his own eyes.

orig.note: Pali dhammacetiya: a monument to the Dhamma. the Buddha's name for the king's reasons.

carryVoice: Your line: why I bow. His reasons were things he'd seen, not things he'd heard. See you tomorrow.
